alternative: a for loop with reassigned variables (Go's only iteration form), the standard fold-style range loop over a slice, or an explicit []T work stack when the recursion is not tail-recursive
implementation_notes: Go's compiler does not implement tail-call optimization - the proposal to add it even for self-recursion only was closed with milestone Unplanned (golang/go#16798) - so a tail-recursive function keeps a frame per step and the pattern's constant-stack promise does not hold. Goroutine stacks are growable rather than fixed, which does not fix this: the recursion still costs memory proportional to depth, just on the heap-backed stack. The realization is the ordinary for loop with mutable state (or a for { } state machine), which is also the form Go readers expect.
idiom_name: for loop with reassigned variables (the compiler does not eliminate tail calls)
pitfalls: Growable stacks hide the problem at small scale: instead of a crash at a fixed limit, a deep tail recursion grows the goroutine stack to megabytes of heap before it fails, so the symptom is memory pressure.
A defer in the recursive frame is not a tail call - deferred calls accumulate and run on the way out - so recursive resource cleanup must become an explicit loop or an enclosing scope.
A recursive goroutine per step (go step(...)) converts stack growth into goroutine count; that is a different resource, not elimination.
